title: Retail Partner Business Review — Market Brief
byline: Prepared by Tia Nelson  |  July 30, 2026  |  Covers BD meeting: Retail Partner Business Review (7/14) — Northgate Pet Supply
recap: Attendees:
Maria Chen (Purina Key Account Manager), Dave Holloway (Category Buyer, Northgate Pet Supply), Renee Ortiz (Purina Field Sales Rep), Kevin Park (Store Operations Lead, Northgate).
Reviewed:
Q2 sell-through data — Pro Plan Adult Shredded Blend and Pro Plan Sport both growing steadily at Northgate. Adult holds primary eye-level placement; Sport sits lower on shelf.
Proposed:
Renee proposed expanding Sport's facing count ahead of fall, paired with in-store demos targeting active-dog owners.
Concern:
Dave flagged inconsistent Sport 30/20 velocity outside hunting/working-dog-community stores and questioned whether the price gap vs. Northgate's private label justifies more shelf space.
Concern:
Kevin cited tight back-stock space ahead of the holiday reset and wants firmer sell-through projections before committing more footprint.
Left:
Fall demo piloted in 15 stores rather than chain-wide. Renee sends store-type-segmented sales data to Dave by August 15. Shelf reset decision revisited in Q4.
signals: Pro Plan Sport 30/20 is explicitly marketed around VO2 max/endurance for canine athletes, hunting dogs, and working dogs — a narrower claim than "active dog owners" broadly (Purina, Vetstreet).
"Lifestyle formulas" for active pets are among the pet-food innovations owners say they're most interested in, signaling real demand for the active-dog category beyond a hunting/working niche.

Private label in specialty pet retail has shifted from a value play to a genuine premium threat: private-label unit sales grew 3.5% in 2024–2025 while national-brand units fell 0.6%; private-label shelf space is up roughly 25% in supermarkets and over 70% of large retailers have launched exclusive pet-food brands; penetration has roughly doubled to ~30% over the past decade (IndexBox, Mordor Intelligence, Business Research Insights).

Private label is increasingly built to match national-brand claims (grain-free, high-protein, functional health), narrowing the differentiation gap Dave is implicitly weighing against Sport's price premium.
implications: Dave's price/shelf-space objection isn't just one buyer being cautious — it tracks a real structural shift where private label is taking share from national brands at retail broadly. Asking for harder proof before expanding Sport's footprint is a rational response to that trend, not resistance to Purina specifically.

Sport's narrow "athlete/hunting/working dog" positioning is a plausible explanation for the inconsistent velocity Dave observed outside those pockets — the product's own framing may be under-indexing the broader "active lifestyle" buyer segment that market data shows is actually growing.

The fall demo plan is well-aligned with data showing lifestyle-formula messaging drives owner interest — but only if the pilot's store selection and messaging target the broader active-lifestyle audience, not just hunting/working-dog-adjacent stores, or it risks reproducing the same velocity gap Dave flagged.
actions: Renee (by Aug 15):

Segment the regional sales data by store audience type — hunting/working-dog-adjacent vs. broader active-lifestyle — not just region, to test whether velocity tracks audience rather than geography. This answers Dave's underlying question with data instead of assumption.
Maria:

When re-pitching shelf space, lead with the private-label share-shift data (private label +3.5% vs. national -0.6%) to reframe the ask as "defend national-brand shelf share before further private-label encroachment" — an argument that serves Northgate's own margin interests, not just Purina's.
Renee/Marketing:

Scope the 15-store demo pilot to include stores outside the hunting/working-dog core, using active-lifestyle messaging rather than sport/hunting-specific framing, to test whether broader positioning improves velocity before the Q4 shelf-reset decision.
Kevin:

Come Q4, pair the sell-through results with a smaller-footprint case-pack option for any expanded facing, addressing the back-stock constraint directly rather than assuming a larger footprint is the only path to more shelf space.

title: Bright Mind Puppy Launch Planning — Market Brief
byline: Prepared by Tia Nelson  |  July 30, 2026  |  Covers BD meeting: Bright Mind Puppy Launch Planning (7/21)
recap: Attendees:
Jordan Ellis (Brand Manager, Pro Plan Puppy Line), Dr. Priya Nair (R&D Lead), Tom Bricker (Packaging Designer), Sam Whitfield (Marketing Coordinator).
Reviewed:
Refreshed Bright Mind Puppy formula with increased DHA for cognitive/neural development; formulation trials met target benchmarks.
Reviewed:
Three packaging concepts with updated colors and clearer DHA callouts — concept 2 was the early favorite and moves into consumer testing.
Proposed:
Q1 2027 launch plan: veterinary clinic seeding plus puppy-training influencer partnerships ahead of retail rollout.
Concern:
Dr. Nair flagged lead-time risk from a single-source overseas fish-oil supplier.
Concern:
Sam flagged that the proposed February launch window overlaps a competitor's planned puppy campaign.
Left:
Dr. Nair to confirm a backup supplier by August 20. Sam to research shifting launch 2–3 weeks earlier. Follow-up meeting tentatively set for late August.
signals: The fish-oil/omega-3 supply chain is under real, industry-wide strain, not a single-supplier quirk: potential shortfalls of roughly 20,000 tonnes this year, with Peruvian anchovy quotas — 35–40% of global fish oil — down 36% in 2026, and tightness projected to persist toward 2033 (ingredientsnetwork.com, nutraingredients.com).

In response, algal-oil DHA sources are gaining real share as a fish-oil substitute — roughly 18–22% of domestic omega-3 supply in 2026, up from under 10% in 2020, with suppliers like dsm-firmenich now marketing microalgal oil specifically as a fish-oil replacement.

DHA-for-cognitive-development is not an open lane: Eukanuba relaunched its puppy line in March 2026 with DHA cognitive-support recipes, and Zignature launched a new early-life puppy formula in April 2026 built around DHA/omega-3 for brain, eye, skin, and coat — both moves predate the proposed Q1 2027 Bright Mind launch.

No evidence surfaced of a Hill's-specific puppy cognitive product or a Hill's puppy campaign timed to Q1 2027 — Hill's cognitive-support marketing (Senior Vitality) is concentrated at the Adult 7+ senior end, not puppies.
implications: Dr. Nair's supply-risk concern is understated, not overstated: this is a multi-year structural shortage, not a one-off. A single backup supplier still sourcing conventional fish oil doesn't fully de-risk the launch — the industry's own hedge is shifting toward algal-oil sourcing, which wasn't part of the meeting's discussion.

Sam's instinct to worry about competitive overlap was aimed at the wrong evidence: no Hill's puppy cognitive launch surfaced, but Eukanuba and Zignature already shipped DHA-cognitive puppy products months ago. The bigger competitive risk isn't one rival's February campaign — it's that "DHA for puppy brain development" is becoming a category-standard claim rather than Bright Mind's exclusive story, which matters more for positioning than for launch date.

Because DHA-cognitive claims are proliferating industry-wide, packaging concept 2's DHA callout may need a more specific, trial-backed hook to stand out, rather than "increased DHA" alone — while the puppy-stage cognitive claim itself remains real white space against Hill's specifically.
actions: Dr. Nair (by Aug 20):

Alongside a backup conventional supplier, evaluate an algal-oil DHA source as a secondary hedge — it's the direction the broader ingredient supply chain is already moving, and it removes exposure to Peruvian anchovy quota volatility rather than just diversifying it.
Sam:

Reframe the competitive research from "avoid one rival's February window" to benchmarking Bright Mind's DHA claim against Eukanuba's and Zignature's already-launched puppy formulas — the launch-date shift matters less than whether Bright Mind's cognitive claim is differentiated once it ships.
Jordan/Tom:

Sharpen packaging concept 2's DHA messaging with a specific, trial-backed claim using Dr. Nair's benchmark data, since competitors have already normalized "DHA for puppy brain development" as a category claim.
Jordan:

Since no Hill's puppy-cognitive product surfaced, protect that white space explicitly in launch messaging — puppy-stage cognitive support, where Hill's is concentrated at the senior end — even as Eukanuba/Zignature contest the broader DHA claim.

title: Veterinary Channel Partnership — Market Brief
byline: Prepared by Tia Nelson  |  July 30, 2026  |  Covers BD meeting: Veterinary Channel Partnership (7/27) — Riverbend Animal Hospital
recap: Attendees:
Alan Restrepo (Purina Veterinary Channel Manager), Dr. Lisa Fenwick (Lead Veterinarian, Riverbend Animal Hospital), Grace Tomlin (Practice Manager, Riverbend).
Reviewed:
Stocking program for Pro Plan Veterinary Diets EN Gastroenteric and HA Hydrolyzed — starting inventory levels, staff training materials, client education handouts.
Noted:
Dr. Fenwick said patient interest in therapeutic diets has grown, but staff lack quick-reference materials to explain formula differences in short appointments.
Concern:
Grace raised upfront inventory cost given limited clinic storage and asked about smaller trial case sizes.
Concern:
Dr. Fenwick noted client confusion between OTC sensitive-stomach formulas and prescription-only Veterinary Diets at checkout.
Left:

Alan to provide smaller starter case sizes for a 60-day trial and develop clearer OTC-vs-prescription signage. Grace to identify checkout-area shelf space for signage. Group reconvenes after the trial.
signals: The US pet veterinary/therapeutic diet market is growing steadily (roughly $11.71B to $12.57B in 2026 domestically; global therapeutic diet market near $30.9B in 2026), driven by rising GI-disorder prevalence, wider pet insurance coverage, and growing vet recommendation of prescription nutrition (Mordor Intelligence, Persistence Market Research).

Vet clinics/hospitals remain the dominant distribution channel — over 65% of therapeutic diet sales originate through the veterinary channel, with hospitals/clinics alone holding roughly a 43% revenue share, underscoring how much a single clinic relationship like Riverbend matters to volume.

Purina already runs a Vet Direct model — letting clinics have prescribed diets shipped directly to the pet owner's home rather than dispensed from clinic shelf stock — as a stated growth lever for its therapeutic segment.

Hill's Prescription Diet Gastrointestinal Biome, built on a proprietary "ActivBiome+" technology, is clinically marketed to help firm loose stool within 24 hours and rebalance gut microbiome — a direct, well-marketed competitor to EN Gastroenteric on the same GI claim.

Hill's runs the identical OTC (Sensitive Stomach & Skin) vs. prescription-only (Prescription Diet) line split that Purina does, and Hill's own ingredient quality has drawn public criticism (pea/legume and filler content) — a credibility gap Purina doesn't share on that specific front.
implications: Grace's storage/inventory objection has a real solution beyond smaller case packs: Purina's own Vet Direct home-delivery model could let Riverbend prescribe EN Gastroenteric/HA Hydrolyzed without holding as much physical stock, directly addressing her stated constraint rather than just shrinking the ask.

Dr. Fenwick's "staff lack quick-reference materials" complaint is more urgent than it sounds given Hill's ActivBiome+ is an actively marketed, clinically-branded rival claim on the exact same GI territory — Riverbend's vet techs need to be able to differentiate EN Gastroenteric from a named competitor product, not just describe general "gut health" benefits.

The OTC-vs-Rx confusion Dr. Fenwick raised isn't Riverbend-specific — Hill's runs the same split and has faced public criticism for unclear claims — meaning generic signage may under-serve the actual need; plain, literal language is likely to travel better than category jargon.
actions: Alan:

Alongside smaller starter case sizes, formally offer Riverbend enrollment in Purina's Vet Direct home-delivery program for EN Gastroenteric/HA Hydrolyzed — it addresses Grace's storage constraint more durably than trial-size inventory alone.
Alan:

Update Riverbend's staff training materials to include a direct, named comparison against Hill's ActivBiome+ (mechanism and clinical claim differences), not just general EN Gastroenteric benefits, so staff have a specific answer when a client asks how it differs from what Hill's markets.
Alan/Grace:

Draft the OTC-vs-prescription signage in plain, literal terms (e.g., "requires a vet prescription") rather than category language — the same confusion shows up wherever this OTC/Rx split exists, so specificity is what resolves it.
Alan:

Track uptake by SKU during the 60-day trial specifically against the GI claim (EN Gastroenteric), given Hill's is actively competing on that exact territory — a soft result there is a competitive signal, not just a stocking-level problem.

title: Sensitive Skin & Stomach Digital Campaign — Market Brief
byline: Prepared by Tia Nelson  |  July 30, 2026  |  Covers BD meeting: Sensitive Skin & Stomach Digital Campaign Planning (7/29)
recap: Attendees:
Nicole Farrow (Digital Marketing Manager), Brian Kessler (Social Media Strategist), Ana Souza (Creative Lead, Meridian Agency), Jordan Ellis (Brand Manager).
Reviewed:

Fall digital campaign for Pro Plan Sensitive Skin & Stomach targeting pet parents managing food sensitivities and skin issues — content calendar across paid social, search, and organic, plus an influencer shortlist.
Reviewed:
Ana's creative concepts built on before-and-after storytelling; Jordan reviewed budget allocation across paid social, search, and influencer spend.
Concern:
Ana pushed back that the draft messaging read too clinical and risked losing emotional engagement.
Concern:
Jordan questioned whether the proposed influencer spend would outperform heavier paid-media investment.
Left:
Ana to revise creative toward warmer, more relatable messaging by August 5. Jordan to finalize the influencer/paid budget split before the next review. Target: mid-September launch.
signals: Pet-specific influencer content substantially outperforms typical paid benchmarks: 10–40% engagement rates per post versus 1–3% for macro/brand-account content; pet-owner audiences follow influencers at a 63% rate and engage with pet content at over 2x the rate of general posts.

Micro-creator, authentic content is what's converting in 2026 — macro-influencer campaigns "drained budgets in 2025 with polished posts that generated likes but failed to move product," while genuine, routine-based reactions from smaller creators are landing with pet owners.

The highest-ROI structure isn't influencer-vs-paid as an either/or: repurposing top-performing creator content into paid social captures 30–50% of campaign ROI that's otherwise left on the table when brands don't secure usage rights upfront.

Hill's — Purina's direct competitor in this exact category (Sensitive Stomach & Skin OTC) — has named pet humanization and emotionally-driven marketing as explicit 2026 growth pillars for parent Colgate-Palmolive, backed by a "Because You're Only Human" campaign and an AI-supported "Omni-Demand Generation" model — the whole category is moving toward warmer, more human-feeling marketing.

Separately, Hill's own ingredient quality (peas, legumes, filler ingredients in its Sensitive Stomach & Skin line) has drawn public criticism — a specific vulnerability Purina isn't exposed to on the same terms.
implications: Ana's pushback on "too clinical" messaging isn't a stylistic preference — it's directionally exactly where the category's highest-performing content and Hill's own stated 2026 strategy are both headed. Sticking with clinical messaging would be working against both the engagement data and the direct competitor's playbook.

Jordan's budget question has a data-backed answer that isn't "pick one": the highest-ROI move is securing usage rights on the influencer shortlist's best content upfront so it can be repurposed as paid social, rather than treating influencer and paid spend as competing line items.

Because Hill's marketing leans on premiumization and "human-grade" positioning while its actual ingredient list draws quality criticism, Purina's creative doesn't need to out-market Hill's on emotional tone alone — it can pair warmer storytelling with a straightforward ingredient-confidence angle, a credibility gap Hill's can't easily close.
actions: Ana (by Aug 5):

Revise creative toward micro-creator-style, authentic before-and-after storytelling rather than polished/macro-style content — matching what the engagement data shows actually converts in this category.
Jordan:

Before finalizing the budget split, build in contractual usage rights for the top-performing influencer content so it can be repurposed as paid social — the single highest-leverage lever in the data (30–50% additional ROI), which changes the influencer-vs-paid framing entirely.
Nicole/Brian:
Prioritize short-form video over static posts across the content calendar, consistent with what's driving discovery and engagement in pet content specifically.
Ana/Nicole:

Where the creative allows, pair warmer emotional storytelling with a plain-spoken ingredient-confidence note — a direct, low-cost contrast against Hill's, whose ingredient quality has drawn public criticism even as its marketing leans heavily on premium/human-grade tone.
